title: Strain-enhanced stretchable molecular ferroelectric acoustic fibers

paper_content.abstract:
Molecular ferroelectrics—hybrid organic-inorga nic architectures that exhibit piezoelectric
coefficients comparable to classic oxide ceramics while offering rich compositional and structural
tunability—have emerged as promising materials for human-interfaced high-frequency acoustic
sensing. Nevertheless, the inherent brittleness and relatively high modulus hinder their practical
deployment on dynamically deformable interfaces. Here, we report stretchable molecular
ferroelectric acoustic fibers fabricated by incorporating molecular ferroelectric
trimethylchloromethyl ammTonium trichlorocadmium (TMCM-CdCl
3
) crystals into flexible
thermoplastic polyurethaRne (TPU) via electrospinning. Intermolecular interactions between
TMCM-CdCl and TPAU, along with the interlocked layered architecture between electrodes and
3
fibers, endow the fiber acoustic sensor with high stretchability (tensile strain >100%), high force
sensing sensitivity (4.36 V/kPa), and wide-frequency acoustic sensing (30–5000 Hz). Crucially, a
strain-induced sensitivity enhancement effect is proposed and verified, where the acoustic
sensitivity of the sensor increases from 15.03 mV/dB to 30.16 mV/dB under strain. Furthermore,
we demonstrate that the acoustic fiber can maintain a high speech recognition accuracy (97.05%)
even for mixed speech data obtained using the acoustic fiber in original and 20% tensile strain
states. This work establishes a route for acoustic sensing at dynamic deformable interface and
advances human-interfaced acoustic applications such as robotic interaction, biomedical
engineering, and virtual reality.
paper_content.introduction:
Sound is ubiquitous in both natural phenomena and human activities, serving as a fundamental
medium for human perception and environmental interaction. Flexible acoustic sensors emulate
this biological function by converting ambient acoustic information into quantifiable electrical
signals (1-3). Compared with conventional rigid devices, their intrinsic flexibility enables both
conformal skin attachment and adaptability to dynamically curved surfaces (4). These devices have
emerged as a focal point of research due to their transformative potential in robotic interaction (5,
6), biomedicine (7, 8), and virtual reality applications (9, 10).

With advances in material science and sensing technologies, various flexible acoustic sensors,
based on the mechanisms of electromagnetic (11), piezoresistive (12), piezocapacitive (13), optical
(14), triboelectric (5), and piezoelectric (15), have been explored for acoustic perception and
intelligent applications. For instance, Yan et al. utilized barium titanate (BTO)/poly(vinylidene
fluoride-co-trifluoroethylene) piezoelectric fibers woven into a conformable acoustic fabric (16).
This smart fabric enables acoustic pulse direction detection and bidirectional acoustic
communication. As applications evolve from requiring simple, flexible scenarios to those
demanding integration with complex, dynamically deforming surfaces or environments (e.g.,
human body interfaces, typically exhibiting >10N% strain), the development of stretchable acoustic
sensors has therefore become imperative (17)I. However, due to fundamental limitations in device
architecture and working principles, Eexisting acoustic sensors (such as piezoresistive and
piezocapacitive types) often require Lcomplex structural designs to achieve real-time acoustic
sensing under dynamic strain. ICn contrast, piezoelectric acoustic sensors rely on thin-film
vibrations induced by acousticI waves for sound detection. This simple yet efficient working
mechanism provides a feasible route toward stretchable acoustic devices (18).

Conventional piezoelectric materials often suffer from a trade-off between electrical performance
and mechanical properties. Inorganic piezoelectric ceramics, represented by PZT and BTO, exhibit
relatively high piezoelectric coefficients (d ) but are limited by excessive rigidity and complicated
33
fabrication processes (19). On the other hand, organic piezoelectric polymers such as PVDF offer
good flexibility, yet their d remain relatively low (20). Molecular ferroelectrics, as a novel class
33
of piezoelectric materials, have garnered significant attention in recent years owing to their
attractive merits, including structurally tunable frameworks, light weight, low acoustic impedance,
and facile crystallization and film formation (21-23). Taking hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite
molecular ferroelectrics as an example, their piezoelectric behavior originates from the ordered
arrangement and interactions of molecular components (e.g., organic cations and inorganic
frameworks) within the crystal lattice (24). These materials combine the advantageous
characteristics of both organic molecules and inorganic frameworks. It is noteworthy that the d
33
values of certain molecular ferroelectric materials have already surpassed those of traditional
inorganic ceramics (25). For example, our group previously reported the hybrid perovskite
organic-inorganic perovskite molecular ferroelectric TMCM-CdCl (TMCM =
3
trimethylchloromethyl ammonium [Me NCH Cl]+) which exhibits a remarkably high d value of
3 2 33
220 pC/N (26). However, it also faces intrinsic brittleness, typically requiring doping strategies to
enable its application in flexible sensors. Compared with inorganic piezoelectric ceramics,
TMCM-CdCl can be mutually dissolved with polymer matrices in solvents. Furthermore, its
3
abundant organic components allow for the formation of strong intermolecular interactions, such
as hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, halogen interactions and other van der Waals forces, with the
polymer matrix (27, 28). Consequently, uniformly dispersed TMCM-CdCl crystallites can form
3
robust interfacial bonding with the polymer matrix, making them less prone to fatigue fracture
under strain while enabling efficient stress transmission for electromechanical transduction. Based
on this composite strategy, significant progress has been made in existing research. For example,
the use of a porous TPU framework loaded with TMCM-CdCl crystals has yielded piezoelectric
3
composite materials with high power output (29). Additionally, TMCM-CdCl /PVP composite
3
fibers prepared via the electrospinning process have been successfully applied in low-frequency
sound recognition (30). These studies have confirmed the application potential of the TMCM-
CdCl and polymer composite system. However, the electromechanical coupling behavior of
3
molecular ferroelectric crystals and polymer matrices under dynamic tensile deformation remains
unexplored, and its underlying mechanisms are still unclear. Furthermore, the interface contact
issues between the composite material and elecNtrodes during dynamic deformation have not yet
been considered.

Herein, we designed stretchable TMECM-CdCl
3
/TPU (TCCT) composite fibers by uniformly
dispersing high-d TMCM-CdCl crLystals into a TPU matrix via electrospinning technology,
33 3
which serves as the piezoelectricC active layer. Utilizing the robust intermolecular interactions
between the crystals and the maItrix effectively improved the mechanical tensile stability of the
fibers. In the sensor architecture, we constructed a dense intermediate layer (interlocked layered
architecture) at the interface between the liquid metal (LM)/TPU electrode and the TCCT fibers
through rational process design. This structure not only ensures a robust connection between the
piezoelectric active layer and the electrodes but also effectively enhances the charge coupling
efficiency of the electrodes. The resulting TCCT sensor demonstrated a pressure sensitivity (4.36
V/kPa) and strain performance (109%). For acoustic sensing, the sound sensitivity of the sensor
under stretched conditions increased to 30.16 mV/dB, twice that in the unstretched state. This
improvement primarily originates from the synergistic effect between the strain-induced intrinsic
piezoelectric enhancement of the crystals and the increased stress transfer efficiency resulting from
the densified fiber network. Notably, stretching enhances the sensor’s ability to recognize
information features within the raw speech signal. Overall, the TCCT sensor with strain-enhanced
perception capability provides a viable strategy for developing next-generation flexible acoustic
sensing devices. These devices can adapt to dynamic and complex environments while maintaining
high sensitivity and stability.

To address the brittleness and inflexibility of molecular ferroelectrics and thereby render the
resulting devices compatible with a broad range of complex working scenarios, we incorporated
TMCM-CdCl crystals into a TPU matrix and fabricated TMCM-CdCl /TPU (TCCT) composite
3 3
fibers as the piezoelectric active layer via electrospinning (Fig. 1a). Multiple molecular
interactions formed between the TMCM-CdCl crystals and TPU, including monopolar
3
interactions and van der Waals forces between the -CH groups, -C=O groups in TPU chains and
3
Cl atoms in [CdCl ]− (27), and halogen bonds and abundant van der Waals forces between Cl atoms
3
in [TMCM]+ ([Me NCH Cl]+) and Cl atoms in [CdCl ]− (31). Moreover, the electrospinning
3 2 3
process simultaneously induces a directional poling alignment between TMCM-CdCl and TPU
3

TCCT fibers.

The electrodes employed stretchable LM/TPU composite polymer as the material. The electrode
solution was spread onto a flat-plate collector, enabling the simultaneous one-side electrode
assembly during the fabrication of the piezoelectric active layer. The assembled bilayer structure
was then placed onto the electrode solution, following slow curing, ultimately formed the complete
sensor with top and bottom electrodes (Fig. 1b). Detailed fabrication procedures are provided in
the Methods. The assembled TCCT sensor features a five-layer architecture, comprising
symmetrically arranged upper and lower porouNs layers, dense intermediate layers and a central
nanofiber layer. During electrode curing anId electrospinning formation, a tightly interlocked
structure develops between the piezoeleEctric nanofiber layer and the porous electrode layer. This
architecture significantly enhances inLterfacial bonding between these layers, ensuring reliable
electrical contact during device strCetching (32).

The pressure-sensing capabilityI of the TCCT sensor is enabled by its core filler, TMCM-CdCl
3
crystals. Under external stress, deformation of the TPU matrix effectively couples to that of the
TMCM-CdCl crystallites, and the compressive deformation of the inorganic [CdCl ]− anionic
3 3
framework induces polarization rotation in the organic [TMCM]+ cations, generating a pronounced
piezoelectric response (Fig. 1c) (33). The authentic crystal structure of the paraelectric phase and
configurations of different polarization orientations are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1b.
Synergistically combining the high d coefficient molecular ferroelectric material with a
33

stretchability to the TCCT sensor. Remarkably, applied strain significantly enhances the sensor’s
acoustic-vibrational sensitivity, demonstrating pronounced advantages for voice recognition

Fabrication and characterization of TCCT sensor
To achieve full sensor stretchability, we engineered stretchable electrodes by blending LM
conductive fillers with a polymer matrix. The LM/TPU electrodes exhibit negligible resistance
change under 200% strain (Supplementary Fig. 10). The TCCT sensor features a sandwich
structure (Fig. 3a, b), comprising two LM/TPU electrodes encapsulating a TCCT fibers. The
porous LM/TPU layers function dually as both conductive electrodes and flexible supporting
substrates. The cross-section EDS mapping (SuNpplementary Fig. 11) identified the middle layer as
TCCT fibers, and the main element is Cl. CrIoss-sectional SEM and optical images revealed the

formed between the electrodes and pLiezoelectric active layer. This integrated structure ensures
effective electrode-to-active-layerC contact under tensile strain. The mechanical properties of the

TCCT fibers, the TCCT fibers with LM/TPU electrodes exhibited higher tensile fracture strain. To
further investigate the strain behavior of TCCT fibers, we fabricated sensor with only a single-
sided electrode. Under progressively increasing strain, the white TCCT fibers maintained
conformal contact with the gray LM/TPU electrode. Upon reaching the fracture limit, the fibers
ruptured while the remaining segments retained strong adhesion to the electrode surface
(Supplementary Fig. 14). Simultaneously, real-time visualization under optical microscopy
confirmed intact interfacial bonding in TCCT sensor during stretching (0–40% strain), with no
observable interfacial delamination (Fig. 3e and Supplementary movie 1). We then established a
mechano-electrical measurement system and implemented multi-layer encapsulation to minimize
interference from triboelectric on piezoelectric voltage during testing (Supplementary Fig. 15) (34).

The resulting air gaps introduce additional parasitic capacitance, which consequently reduces
induced charge at the electrodes. In contrast, the LM/TPU electrode design in TCCT sensor
effectively enhances charge collection efficiency by both eliminating interlayer air gaps and
enlarging contact area through its interlocked architecture—thereby significantly improving the

voltage variation (ΔU) to applied pressure change (ΔP) under stable operating conditions. The
sensitivity formula is expressed as S = ΔU/ΔP. As shown in Fig. 3h, within the 0-6 kPa pressure
range, the LM/TPU electrodes configuration achieved a voltage sensitivity of 4.36 V/kPa,
demonstrating significant superiority over conventional Al electrode configuration (see
Supplementary information for calculation details and the data listed in Table 2). Under distinct
pressures (0.5, 1 and 4 kPa), the TCCT sensor generated voltage waveforms with progressively
increasing amplitude while maintaining signal stability (Supplementary Fig. 23). We evaluated the
frequency stability of the TCCT sensor at 1–3 Hz, and the experimental results showed that its
output voltage could maintain stability (Fig. 3i). The TCCT sensor exhibits a response time of
0.03 s, which corresponds to the duration required for the voltage to rise from 10% to 90%
(Supplementary Fig. 24). Durability testing at 0.5 kPa demonstrates preserved waveform integrity
through 7,500 cycles, confirming long-term operational reliability (Supplementary Fig. 25). When
benchmarked against previously reported flexible ferroelectric sensors incorporating inorganic(37),
organic(38-42), and hybrid molecular ferroelectric materials (43, 44) (Fig. 3j, Supplementary
Table 1), the TCCT sensor exhibits exceptional performance in both sensitivity and tensile strain
tolerance. This dual advantage enables precise detection of low-pressure vibrations (e.g., acoustic
signals) and seamless adaptability to stretchable scenarios.

Responses to acoustic forces
Acoustic waves belong to low-pressure vibrational stimuli. To verify the low-pressure detection
capability of the TCCT sensor, we constructed an acoustic testing system (Fig. 4a). In this system,
a sound controller generated sound waves with specific frequency and amplitude, a loudspeaker
served as the sound source, and the data storagNe unit recorded the response voltage generated by
the TCCT sensor. One end of the TCCT sensIor and its lead wire were fixed to a support fixture,
constituting a rigid constraint, while the Eother end was connected to PI tape secured to a fixture on
the opposite side, forming an elasticL constraint (Supplementary Fig. 26). The rigid constraint
suppressed interference from lead Cvibrations during acoustic wave acquisition, whereas the elastic
constraint permited micro-deforImation of the sensor under sound pressure, preserving acoustic
response sensitivity. The sound wave is a sine wave with a defined frequency and decibel level.
Under constant 80 dB pure-tone excitation, the TCCT sensor demonstrated good acoustic response
characteristics across the 30–5000 Hz frequency range (Fig. 4b). Subsequently, we investigated
the influence of strain on the sensor’s acousto-electric conversion capability under an 80 dB and
100 Hz acoustic field (Supplementary Fig. 27). The results showed that the output voltage of the
TCCT sensor continued to increase with strain (0–40% strain), but the rate of voltage rise slowed
significantly once strain exceeded 20%. Therefore, to clearly demonstrate the improvement
resulting from stretching, subsequent experiments focused on the 0–20% strain range. Across
varying acoustic frequencies (30–5000 Hz) and decibel levels (70–100 dB), the TCCT sensor
under 20% strain exhibits significantly superior acoustoelectric conversion capability and acoustic
pressure sensitivity compared with those at 0% and 10% strain (Fig. 4c, d). Original voltage
waveforms are documented in Supplementary Fig. 28 and Fig. 29. Stretching enhances the
sensitivity of the TCCT sensor, which exhibited stable linearity with strain-dependent
enhancement of acoustic sensitivity. Compared with its state before stretching, the acoustic wave
sensitivity of the stretched TCCT sensor increases to 30.16 mV/dB. Fig. 4e elucidates the
mechanism of strain-enhanced piezoelectric response. Under the same acoustic excitation, lateral
stretching induces a certain strain in the TMCM-CdCl crystals within the fibers (Supplementary
3
Fig. 30, with material parameters provided in Table 3), which directly enhances the intrinsic
piezoelectric response of the crystals (45). Simultaneously, it promotes a denser internal structure
of the TCCT fibers (Supplementary Fig. 31). The compact structure improves the mechanical
coupling and stress transfer efficiency between the fibers (46), ensuring that external loads are
more effectively transmitted to the crystals embedded in the TPU matrix. The synergistic effect of
strain-induced enhancement of the intrinsic piezoelectric response of the crystals and improved
stress transfer efficiency resulting from the optimized fiber network structure enhances the
electromechanical conversion efficiency of the TCCT sensor, resulting in a significant increase in
surface charge density and output voltage. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), a critical parameter for
assessing output signal quality, is defined as the ratio of useful signal power to background noise
power under specified operating conditions, expressed as SNR = 20log(V /V ). Within the
output noise
0–1.3 Pa sound pressure range, the strained TCCT sensor demonstrated higher SNR values
compared to its unstrained state (Fig. 4f). Benchmarked against state-of-the-art flexible
piezoelectric acoustic sensors (Fig. 4g) (2, 15, 16, 47-51), the TCCT sensor achieves a broader
dynamic detection range (30–5000 Hz) that fully encompasses the human voice frequency
spectrum (300–3400 Hz). Although comparison results indicate that some flexible piezoelectric
acoustic sensors do outperform the current TCCNT sensor in terms of frequency response range, the
TCCT sensor possesses a strain-enhancedI acoustic sensing capability, which validates its
significant advantages for dynamic and dEifferent voice detection applications.

Applications and demonstrationCs
Voice information represents a pIrimary means of human interaction. We simulated the complete
human auditory perception and recognition process by integrating TCCT sensor with deep learning
algorithms (Fig. 5a). The TCCT sensor mimics the human auditory mechanism by converting
external acoustic stimuli into electrical signals. Deep learning algorithms then process the sensor
data, emulating the brain’s capacity to analyze, process, and recognize acoustic signals.
Comparative analysis of the piezoelectric signals acquired by the commercial sensor (LDT0-028K)
and the TCCT sensor during continuous audio playback demonstrated that the TCCT sensor
achieves high fidelity in reconstructing the original waveform (Fig. 5b and Supplementary movie
2). Further time-frequency analysis via short-time Fourier transform (STFT) revealed that the
TCCT sensor completely preserved the complex time-varying frequency characteristics of the
original speech within the 0–2000 Hz range, whereas the commercial sensor exhibited severe
information loss (Fig. 5c). Furthermore, a comparison of the piezoelectric signals collected by the
TCCT sensor before and after stretching revealed a significant increase in output voltage, along
with an improvement in its high-frequency response capability (Supplementary Fig. 32). Fast
Fourier transform (FFT) analysis revealed that the TCCT sensor outperformed commercial sensor
in capturing and reconstructing key frequency components across the 0-1000 Hz spectrum
(Supplementary Fig. 33). Under 20% strain, the sensor enabled partial reconstruction of frequency
components within the 1000–2000 Hz band, albeit with variations in the amplitude ratios of certain
subtle spectral peaks owing to the intrinsic damping of the device. Concurrently, a shift of the peak
response toward higher frequencies was observed. This phenomenon originated from strain-
induced changes in the elastic stiffness of the TCCT sensor, leading to an increase in high-
frequency components (Supplementary note 2). Although the change in stiffness caused by
stretching introduces slight resonance peak shifts, the enhancement in sensitivity plays a decisive
role in improving the spectral consistency with the original signal. Specifically, under 20% strain,
the acoustic response characteristics of the TCCT sensor are enhanced. Compared with the
unstretched state, the stretched sensor can more effectively capture the high-frequency details of
the original sound signal. This strain-enabled rapid frequency response tuning allows
customization of sensitivity ranges for targeted applications, demonstrating exceptional versatility
in acoustic detection.

To evaluate the impact of strain on speech signal feature acquisition by TCCT sensor, we captured
acoustic signals from sensors under before-stretching and after-stretching conditions (Fig. 5d and
Supplementary Fig. 34). We tested words such as Science and Nature, and the TCCT sensor was
able to accurately reconstruct the speech signals without degradation even under stretching
deformation. The strained state exhibited significantly amplified voltage amplitudes while
preserving waveform characteristics with onlyN minor deviations. Simultaneously, we employed
deep learning techniques to classify and reIcognize basic speech elements, utilizing a hybrid
architecture of convolutional neural neEtworks (CNN) and long short-term memory (LSTM)
networks to process the test data (FigL. 5e). Here, the CNN extracts local features of the speech
signal, filters out noise, and capturCes key acoustic patterns effectively. The LSTM is designed for
processing sequential data and cIan model the temporal dependencies in speech. The combination
of CNN and LSTM enhances the robustness of the model in recognizing speech under different
strain conditions. The network employs three one-dimensional convolutional modules (channel
configuration: 128-256-512, kernel size: 5) for local acoustic feature extraction. A bidirectional
LSTM layer (128→64 units) captures temporal dependencies, where the initial 128-unit layer
preserves sequence states and the subsequent 64-unit layer outputs global contextual features. Final
classification is performed through a fully connected layer. Using t-distributed stochastic neighbor
embedding (t-SNE), we visualized TCCT sensor data under varying stretching conditions in a low-
dimensional space. Distinct clustering was observed for signals acquired in the unstretched state
and stretched state (Fig. 5f, Supplementary Fig. 35a). Clear clustering persists when combining
before-stretching and after-stretching data (Fig. 5g). The confusion matrix synthesizes the
classification accuracy, and the recognition accuracy of the mixed data can reach 97.05% (Fig. 5h).
Although the prediction accuracy for the mixed data decreased compared to that in unstretched
and stretched states alone (Fig. 5i and Supplementary Fig. 35b-c), it maintained distinct clustering
and high recognition accuracy. This demonstrates the TCCT sensor’s capability to precisely
reconstruct speech signal features under mechanical stretching.

under reduced pressure to yield TMCM-Cl. 50 mmol TMCM-Cl and 50 mmol CdCl were

crystals in 10 mL of DMF (Aladdin, GC grade >99.9%) under continuous heating and stirring at

3
and continuous stirring at 60 °C for 5 h to obtain a transparent spinning solution. The prepared
spinning solution was loaded into a syringe with a metallic needle (Size: No. 19). A voltage of 20
kV was applied to the needle tip with a syringe feed rate of 0.65 mL h-1. The syringe underwent

A flat-plate collector was positioned approximIately 120 mm from the needle to collect deposited
TMCM-CdCl
3
/TPU composite nanofEibers. Fibers’ thickness was tailored by varying
electrospinning duration.

Device fabrication of TCCT seInsor
A TPU solution was prepared by dissolving 3 g TPU in 30 mL of DMF with continuous heating
and stirring at 60 °C for 5 h. Subsequently, 3 g of liquid metal (LM, 75% Ga, 25% In) was added
to the TPU solution. The mixture underwent probe sonication (KC-600W, 75%) in a room-
temperature water bath for 0.5 h to yield a uniformly dispersed LM/TPU electrode composite
solution. Prior to electrospinning the TCCT fibers, a certain amount of (1.0–1.5 mL) the electrode
composite solution was transferred into a pre-fabricated rectangular Excoflex mold (length × width:
60 mm × 30 mm) positioned on the flat-plate collector. The mold was maintained at 40 °C and 50%
relative humidity for 0.25 h to allow surface DMF evaporation. Subsequently, environmental
conditions were adjusted to 40 °C and 20% humidity to initiate the electrospinning process
(parameters as previously described), enabling direct deposition of the TCCT nanofiber membrane
onto the pre-cured electrode layer. Following electrospinning, TCCT fibers with unilateral
LM/TPU electrodes were obtained. The resulting fibers underwent vacuum drying at 40 °C for 12

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
General commeents:
The manuscript reports a composite strategy by combining molecular ferroelectric fibers with low-modulus polymer fibers
through electrospinning to overcome brittleness. However, both the strategy and the fabrication technique are rather
conventional and do not provide a clear breakthrough. Moreover, the work lacks in-depth characterization to elucidate the
core mechanism of sensitivity enhancement, leaving key claims insufficiently substantiated. In addition, there are
inconsistencies in data reporting, contradictions in interpretation, and issues with data presentation that reduce the overall
clarity and rigor of the study. Taken together, these issues seriously undermine the novelty and reliability of the work, and in
its current form, the manuscript is not suitable for publication.
My specific concerns are outlined below:
1. There is an inconsistency in the reported sensitivity. The Abstract and the last paragraph of the Introduction state 4.69 V
kPa⁻¹, whereas the main text and the Conclusion cite 4.36 V kPa⁻¹. This inconsistency reduces clarity and should be
corrected and justified.
2. The claim that TMCM-CdCl3 preserves its molecular ferroelectricity in the TPU composite is unconvincing. While the
authors emphasize multiple intermolecular interactions with TPU, such interactions could also disrupt the crystalline
structure required for ferroelectricity. This is reflected in Figure 2g, where the original split diffraction peaks merge after
embedding. Moreover, the SHG signal in Figure 2i is insufficient, as it can result from interfacial polarization or partial dipole
alignment rather than intrinsic ferroelectricity. Without corroborating evidence (e.g., P-E loops or domain imaging), the
conclusion is unsupported.
3. In Figure 2g, the XRD patterns of the TCCT composite clearly show the characteristic diffraction peaks of TMCM-CdCl3,
confirming its crystalline presence. However, in Figure 2h, the corresponding FTIR spectrum displays the Cl-related
vibrational features only very weakly, despite the nominally identical filler content. This inconsistency raises questions about
the actual structural and chemical state of TMCM-CdCl₃ in the TPU matrix. The authors should clarify this discrepancy and
provide further evidence (e.g., deconvoluted FTIR spectra, Raman analysis).
4. In Figure 2k, the stress-strain curves show unexpected trends: the modulus at 1 wt% appears higher than at 3 wt%, and
the ultimate stress at 10 wt% is similar to 5 wt%. These inconsistencies are counterintuitive, and the authors should clarify
the reasons for this behavior.
5. In Page 8, line 256-257, the authors attribute reduced output at 10 wt% to aggregation and uneven polarization. However,
they previously emphasized that strong interactions with TPU ensure uniform dispersion, which is contradictory. At such a
low loading, severe aggregation is unlikely, raising doubts about the stability of the ferroelectric polarization within the
composite. The authors should clarify this inconsistency.
6. In Figure 3g, LM/TPU is the main system, yet the authors provide full loading-dependent data only for Al/TPU, while
LM/TPU is represented by a single 5 wt% point. Since Al is merely a reference, one dataset would suffice; the
comprehensive trend should have been shown for LM/TPU. Please clarify this data selection.
7. In Figure 3h, the pressure-dependent voltage responses already encompass the information that is later repeated in
Figure 3i. The latter appears redundant, as it does not add new insights beyond the linear plots. The authors should justify
the necessity of Figure 3i or consider moving it to the Supporting Information.
8. In Figure 4e, the underlying mechanism is explained in Note 2, which attributes the sensitivity enhancement solely to
cross-sectional reduction and stress increase. This explanation appears highly idealized for an electrospun fibrous mat,
which is porous and anisotropic. The definition of an “effective cross-section” is not straightforward, and stress distribution is
likely non-uniform due to fiber orientation and interfacial constraints. Moreover, potential variations in the piezoelectric
coefficient (d₃₁) under strain, as well as the trade-off between sensitivity enhancement and frequency shift, are not
addressed. The authors should provide experimental evidence (e.g., cross-sectional imaging, finite-element simulations, or
polarization analysis) to support the assumptions behind equations (S5–S8).
9. In Figures 5b and 5c, the original sound signal and the sensor outputs are visibly different. Supplementary Fig. 19 further
shows that the original signal has a clear feature at 600-700 Hz, while the TCCT sensor, with or without strain, exhibits only
weak response in this range. This indicates significant distortion and undermines the claim of faithful sound reproduction.
The authors should address this limitation directly.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The scope of the paper entitled "Strain-Enhanced Stretchable Molecular Ferroelectric Acoustic Fiber" presents an acoustic
sensor fabricated through electrospinning technology by integrating molecular ferroelectric crystal TMCM-CdCl3 with
thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), demonstrating high stretchability (>100% strain) and piezoelectric response (4.69 V/kPa).
However, the novelty of the material system (TMCM-CdCl3/TPU) and the electrospinning fabrication process should be
more clearly stated. The proposed strain-enhancement mechanism needs sufficient experimental evidence and rigorous
validation. The following comments should be addressed by major revision before this paper is suitable for publication in
Nature Communications.
1. The authors emphasize that the molecular ferroelectric material TMCM-CdCl3 exhibits a high piezoelectric coefficient and
rich tunability, positioning it as a key solution to the application bottlenecks of traditional piezoelectric materials in flexible
acoustic sensing. However, composite systems of TMCM-CdCl3 with polymer matrices, including TPU, have been
previously reported (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 8636), and the device performance has no significant improvements.
Furthermore, electrospun fibers integrating TMCM-CdCl3 with polymers have been utilized in acoustic sensors (Adv. Mater.
2025, 37, 24092). The authors must therefore more clearly and forcefully articulate the novelty and distinctiveness of their
work relative to these prior studies.
2. The authors' claim that "This improvement primarily originates from the strain-induced stress concentration effect" is
currently supported only by the macroscopic electrical output of the device and a theoretical formulation. To strengthen this
conclusion, additional experimental evidence is recommended.
3. The presented cyclic tensile stability tests yield excellent results. However, for practical deployment, the sensor must
withstand environmental challenges such as varying temperature and humidity. Specifically, the stability of the water-soluble
TMCM-CdCl3 component requires thorough investigation, particularly regarding potential dissolution and recrystallization
under cyclic humidity conditions and overall performance retention in high-humidity environments.
4. The authors compare the sensor performance of Al electrodes with LM/TPU electrodes, attributing the inferior
performance of the Al electrodes to the formation of an air gap at the interface with the TCCT electrospun film. The rationale
for selecting Al as the benchmark for comparison should be explicitly stated. Additionally, to more directly address the air-
gap issue, a control experiment involving the deposition of Al or other metal electrodes directly onto the TCCT film should be
conducted, and how about its performance.
5. The authors repeatedly emphasize the critical role of the interlocked intermediate layer. However, the formation
mechanism of this layer and its specific interaction with the piezoelectric layer remain unclear. Experimental evidence and
characterization detailing the layer's formation process and interface properties are required to support these claims.
6. The molecular ferroelectric material TMCM-CdCl3, which possesses a high piezoelectric coefficient (d33 = 220 pC/N),
was incorporated into a TPU matrix to fabricate composite fibers. It is crucial to investigate whether this fabrication process
compromises its piezoelectric coefficient.
7. The authors state in both the Introduction and Conclusion that the TCCT fiber exhibits excellent tensile properties, citing a
maximum strain of 102%. However, the corresponding tensile data and analysis appear to be absent from the Results and
Discussion section.
8. The authors claim in Figure 4g that the TCCT sensor achieves a wider frequency detection range compared to the current
state-of-the-art piezoelectric acoustic sensors. However, the literature survey appears incomplete. Several recent reports on
piezoelectric acoustic sensors with broad frequency detection ranges appear to have been overlooked (e.g., Nano Energy
2025, 143, 111312; Adv. Funct. Mater. 2024, 34, 2312699; Nature 2022, 603, 616; Nano Energy 2022, 101, 107610).
9. The authors investigate the effect of strain on the sensor's acoustoelectric conversion capability, concluding that 20%
strain yields the maximum voltage output. This conclusion, however, is based on data from only three strain states (0%,
10%, and 20%). Whether a higher strain could yield a greater response
10. The macroscopic deformation of the piezoelectric fiber during stretching will inevitably generate a significant strain-
induced electrical signal. Will there be any interaction or interference between this strain-induced signal and the target
acoustic signal?
11. The claim that "under 20% strain, the TCCT sensor exhibits amplified response characteristics at higher frequencies"
requires substantiation. This claim is not convincingly supported by the data presented in Figure 4c, which shows negligible
differences in the high-frequency voltage output across the different strain states. To robustly support this conclusion,
additional data characterizing the frequency response under various strain states is essential (e.g., modal analysis).
12. Visual inspection of Figures 5b and 5c suggests that the piezoelectric signal captured before straining aligns more
closely with the original audio waveform and exhibits finer acoustic details compared to the signal after straining. This
observation appears to contradict the central claim that strain enhances sensing performance.
13. Figure 5f and 5g present the data before straining and a mixture of pre- and post-straining data, respectively. However,
the dataset corresponding solely to the post-straining state is missing, which is crucial for a direct evaluation of the strain's
effect. Furthermore, the observed decline in accuracy for the mixed dataset requires a clear explanation.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript presents stretchable molecular ferroelectric acoustic fibers with strain-enhanced sound perception
capabilities. The fibers exhibit exceptional speech recognition capabilities, with enhanced sensitivity as strain increases.
This study could be interesting for the audience working on molecular ferroelectrics. I recommend the publication of the
manuscript in Nature Communications, while there are some issues have to be addressed first.
1. The authors used a class of hybrid organic-inorganic molecular perovskite ferroelectrics. Considering the broad
readership of Nature Communications, the authors are suggested to add a description in the appropriate place within the
main text about the advantages of molecular ferroelectrics when compared to traditional piezoelectric materials like PZT,
BTO, and PVDF.
2. The manuscript introduces a molecular ferroelectric composite material prepared by incorporating TMCM-CdCl3 into a
thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) matrix. During the spinning process, the electrode layer is assembled to achieve the
fabrication of a stretchable ferroelectric acoustic device. What are the differences and advantages of the molecular
ferroelectric composite materials and device fabrication method proposed in the manuscript compared to previously reported
piezoelectric acoustic devices?
3. The d33 of TMCM-CdCl3 is 220 pC/N. What is the d33 of TPU/TMCM-CdCl3 (TCCT) composite fibers at different
contents of TMCM-CdCl3? Are the piezoelectric coefficients measured by electrical resonance method which is
recommended by IEEE Standard on Piezoelectricity.
4. Response time is an important parameter in molecular ferroelectric acoustic fibers. How is the response time of the
piezoelectric output of the molecular ferroelectric fibers?
5. Under constant pressure, what is the response trend of the ferroelectric acoustic fibers across different frequencies?
6. Please explain why this neural network model was chosen to be used over others. Considering the broad multi-
disciplinary readers, the author should give the brief necessary background.
7. Some spelling and format mistakes should be corrected. For example, Line 181 on Page 6, and Line 564 on Page 19. The
authors have to carefully check the English throughout the manuscript.

levels of stretching strain. This demonstrates the distinct practical advantages of the
device in complex real‑world wearing scenarios-such as those involving skin
deformation during movement.
